entries.text: Last DSE paper today. Everyone went to celebrate in Mong Kok and I went along, but I felt strangely empty. For six years the plan was just “get through the exam”. Now there's no plan. What am I supposed to want next?

content.headline: The exams ended, and so did the plan
content.recap: You wrote that your last DSE paper was today. You went out to celebrate with everyone, but felt strangely empty, because for six years the only plan was getting through the exam.

analysis.title: Empty after a long push
analysis.text: It might be that the emptiness is what's left when a goal you carried for years suddenly disappears. That's tiredness and space, not failure.
analysis.quote: I felt strangely empty

analysis.title: A new question, not an answer
analysis.text: You're asking what to want next. You don't need to answer it this week; noticing the question is already a start.
analysis.quote: What am I supposed to want next?

challenge.cause: For six years the plan was decided for you, so having nothing scheduled can feel like falling, even though it's just a pause.

advice.text: Give yourself a week with no plan on purpose. Do things you've postponed, and write down anything that makes you lose track of time.
advice.why: You asked what to want next; small clues come before big answers.

content.encouragement: You went out with everyone even though you felt empty. You didn't hide from the day.

steps.text: Sleep in tomorrow without setting an alarm
steps.why: Six years of pressure deserves a slow morning.

steps.text: List three things you postponed because of the DSE
steps.why: Clues about what you want often hide there.

steps.text: Message one friend to plan something fun, not useful

openQuestions: What am I supposed to want next?

entries.text: Hiked Dragon's Back with my cousin. We didn't talk about results or the future at all, just snacks and the view. First day in weeks my head felt quiet.

content.headline: A hike that didn't need to be useful
content.recap: You hiked Dragon's Back with your cousin. You didn't talk about results or the future, and it was the first day in weeks that your head felt quiet.

analysis.title: Quiet came from being outside
analysis.text: It might be that moving and being outdoors gives your mind a break that scrolling doesn't.
analysis.quote: First day in weeks my head felt quiet

analysis.title: A day without the future in it
analysis.text: Not talking about results seems to have been part of what made it restful.
analysis.quote: We didn't talk about results or the future at all

challenge.cause: A good day. The only thing to notice is what made it good.

advice.text: Keep one outdoor afternoon a week while you wait for results.
advice.why: It was the first day in weeks your head felt quiet.

content.encouragement: You said yes to a plan that had no purpose except a good day. That's a skill worth keeping.

steps.text: Save a photo from the hike as your lock screen
steps.why: A small reminder of the quiet.

steps.text: Thank your cousin for the day
steps.why: Good days are worth saying out loud.

steps.text: Pick the next trail you'd like to try

entries.text: Results came out. Good enough for business, and Mum says business is the safer choice. I reordered my choices mostly by what my score fits. I don't hate it. I just don't feel anything about it, and I don't know if that's normal.

content.headline: Results day: good enough, but not a reason
content.recap: Your results came out, good enough for business, and your mum thinks business is the safer choice. You reordered your choices mostly by what your score fits, and you wrote that you don't feel anything about it.

analysis.title: Neutral is information too
analysis.text: Not feeling anything about a choice might mean it hasn't become yours yet, not that it's wrong.
analysis.quote: I just don't feel anything about it

analysis.title: A safe choice, made under pressure
analysis.text: It sounds like the decision was shaped by scores and by what feels safe to your family. That's common, and it can still turn into something you care about.
analysis.quote: Mum says business is the safer choice

challenge.issue: Choosing a major without feeling anything
challenge.cause: The choice was made from your score and safety, so there hasn't been a moment yet where it felt like your own.

advice.text: Before term starts, look for one course or society inside business that sounds a little interesting. You don't need passion yet, just one thread to pull.
advice.why: You said you don't feel anything about it yet.

content.encouragement: You were honest with yourself on a day when it would have been easier to say “it's fine”.

steps.text: Read the course list and star one module that sounds interesting
Tell Mum one thing you're unsure about
steps.why: She can only help with what she knows.

steps.text: Go for a walk after dinner

openQuestions: Is it normal not to feel anything about my major?

entries.text: Hei is leaving for Manchester, Ching got into a uni in Taiwan, Sam is going to a different uni here. Our group of four will be in four places. Everyone seems excited about their plans and I'm just going where my results took me.

content.headline: Four friends, four different places
content.recap: You wrote that Hei is going to Manchester, Ching to Taiwan and Sam to another university in Hong Kong, so your group of four will be in four different places. Everyone seems excited, and you feel like you're just going where your results took you.

analysis.title: A group that's changing shape
analysis.text: It might be the change in the group, more than the plans themselves, that feels heavy.
analysis.quote: Our group of four will be in four places

analysis.title: Measuring by excitement
analysis.text: Their excitement is visible; their doubts probably aren't. Comparing your inside with their outside can make you feel behind.
analysis.quote: I'm just going where my results took me

challenge.issue: Comparing your path with your friends'
challenge.cause: Everyone is announcing plans at the same moment, and yours doesn't come with a story yet.

advice.text: Plan one last evening together before everyone leaves, and ask each friend what they're nervous about.
advice.why: Excited plans often hide nervous ones, too.

content.encouragement: You care about this group enough to notice it changing. That kind of loyalty travels with you.

steps.text: Suggest a date for one last dinner with the four of you
Write one thing you're curious about at uni
Mute the group's story updates for tonight

entries.text: Got the BBA offer today. Mum was so relieved she cried a bit. I'm relieved too. But when people ask “what do you want to do with business?” I have no answer.

content.headline: The offer came: relief, and a question mark
content.recap: You got the BBA offer. Your mum was so relieved she cried a bit, and you're relieved too. But when people ask what you want to do with business, you have no answer.

analysis.title: Two things can be true
analysis.text: Relief and uncertainty arrived together. Neither cancels the other.
analysis.quote: I'm relieved too

analysis.title: You don't owe anyone an answer yet
analysis.text: It might help to remember that most first-years don't know either. The question is fair; the deadline people imply isn't real.
analysis.quote: I have no answer

challenge.issue: Being asked for a plan you don't have
challenge.cause: People ask out of habit, and the question makes it feel like you should already know.

advice.text: Prepare one honest, easy reply for when people ask, like “I'm going to explore first”. It's true, and it takes the pressure off.
advice.why: You wrote that you have no answer.

content.encouragement: You let yourself feel relieved. After this year, that matters.

steps.text: Write your one-line answer to “what will you do with it?”
steps.why: Ready for the next time someone asks.

steps.text: Celebrate the offer with Mum, properly
Look up two societies at your new uni

openQuestions: What do I want to do with business?

entries.text: Saw Hei off at the airport tonight. On the bus home I realised I'll start uni without knowing a single person there. I kept rereading our old photos.

content.headline: Saying goodbye at the airport
content.recap: You saw Hei off at the airport tonight. On the bus home you realised you'll start university without knowing anyone there, and you kept rereading old photos.

analysis.title: Missing someone before term starts
analysis.text: It might be that rereading the photos was a way to stay close to something that's changing.
analysis.quote: I kept rereading our old photos

analysis.title: Starting from zero
analysis.text: Walking into a place where you know no one is genuinely hard. It's also the most common way a first year begins.
analysis.quote: without knowing a single person there

challenge.cause: Your closest friends are leaving at the same time you're starting over, so the gap feels bigger.

advice.text: Choose one orientation event to go to, and decide beforehand that talking to one person counts as a success.
advice.why: You'll start without knowing anyone, so one person is a real start.

content.encouragement: You went to the airport. Showing up for a friend on a hard night says a lot about you.

steps.text: Send Hei a message for when the plane lands
Pick one orientation event to attend
Get to bed before 1am
steps.why: Big feelings are heavier when tired.

entries.text: Orientation day. Hundreds of people, cheers, games. Everyone was shouting and I just smiled and followed. I talked to maybe two people and I don't remember their names. Came home exhausted from pretending to be fine.

content.headline: Orientation was loud, and you felt invisible
content.recap: You went to orientation: hundreds of people, cheers and games. You smiled and followed along, talked to maybe two people, and came home exhausted from pretending to be fine.

analysis.title: Tired from performing
analysis.text: It might be that keeping a smile on in a loud crowd took more energy than the games themselves.
analysis.quote: exhausted from pretending to be fine

analysis.title: Two people is not zero
analysis.text: You still talked to two people on a day designed for extroverts.
analysis.quote: I talked to maybe two people

challenge.issue: Crowds make it hard to connect
challenge.cause: Big loud events reward people who are comfortable shouting; quieter people usually connect better in small groups.

advice.text: Look for small-group settings this week: a tutorial, a society with a hands-on activity, a lunch with one person.
advice.why: Two conversations happened even in the noise.

content.encouragement: You went, stayed, and talked to two people. That's a real first day.

steps.text: Find one small-group activity this week
Have a quiet dinner on your own terms
Say hi to someone you recognise from orientation

entries.text: First group project. The other four already know each other from the same hall. They were nice but I felt like a guest in their group. I did my part well though, the slide I made was the one the tutor liked.

content.headline: A group project with four strangers
content.recap: Your first group project is with four people who already know each other from hall. They were nice, but you felt like a guest. Your slide was the one the tutor liked.

analysis.title: Outside an existing circle
analysis.text: Feeling like a guest might be about joining a group that formed before you arrived, not about you.
analysis.quote: I felt like a guest in their group

analysis.title: Your work spoke for you
analysis.text: On a day you felt on the outside, you still did good work that got noticed.
analysis.quote: the slide I made was the one the tutor liked

challenge.issue: Joining a group that already exists
challenge.cause: They share a hall and a routine, so their closeness came from time together, which you haven't had yet.

advice.text: Suggest one small thing to the group, like getting food after the next meeting. Shared time is how you stop being a guest.
advice.why: Their closeness came from time together.

content.encouragement: Your slide was the one the tutor liked. You brought something real.

steps.text: Suggest grabbing food after the next meeting
Write down what you liked about making that slide
steps.why: A clue about what you enjoy.

steps.text: Take a break from screens before bed

good_at: making a slide the tutor liked

entries.text:
Third week of uni. Everyone already seems to have their group. At lunch I sat alone again and pretended to be busy on my phone. In secondary school I never had to think about who to eat with. My friends are all at different unis now and our group chat is getting quieter. I picked this major because my results fit, not because I really wanted it. Sometimes I wonder if I'm even in the right place.

其實我好想識多啲朋友，但係唔知點樣開始。將來想做咩，我都仲未知。

content.headline: Three weeks in, and still looking for your people
content.recap: You wrote that three weeks into uni, everyone seems to have found their group, and you ate lunch alone again, pretending to be busy on your phone. Your school friends are at different unis, the group chat is getting quieter, and you're not sure this major is really yours. You also said you'd like to make more friends, but don't know where to start.

analysis.title: Your whole world reset at once
analysis.text: It might be less about you and more about timing: a new campus, no shared routine yet, and your old friends scattered, all in the same few weeks. Many first-years are quietly looking for their people right now, even the ones who look settled.
analysis.quote: My friends are all at different unis now

analysis.title: Two big questions got tangled
analysis.text: Feeling alone and doubting your major showed up in the same entry. Loneliness might be making the bigger question, what you want to do, feel more urgent than it needs to be this week.
analysis.quote: 將來想做咩，我都仲未知

challenge.issue: Feeling alone in a brand-new place
challenge.cause: Your social world changed all at once, and the built-in friendships of secondary school are gone. Feeling lonely in the first weeks is a very common part of that change. It isn't a sign that something is wrong with you.

advice.text: Pick one society or activity you're genuinely curious about, not the one that looks best, and go to one session this week. Uni friendships usually grow from doing something together again and again, more than from one perfect conversation. A simple question about the activity is enough to start.
advice.why: You said you want to make friends but don't know where to start.

content.encouragement: You named exactly what's hard: lunch, the quiet group chat, the major. Not just “everything”. Knowing which piece hurts is how you start changing one of them.

steps.text: Star two societies you're genuinely curious about
steps.why: Start from interest, not from what looks impressive.

steps.text: Ask one classmate a question after tutorial
steps.why: Small, low-stakes contact is how most friendships start.

steps.text: Send an old friend a voice message about your week
steps.why: The group chat went quiet, but the friendships didn't end.

openQuestions: Am I in the right place?

remember.text: Just started university; school friends went to other unis
Picked the major for the results, still unsure about it

entries.text: Went to the photography society's first walk in Sham Shui Po. I almost turned back at the door. Stayed. Didn't talk much, but a girl called Wing showed me how she shoots shop signs at night. I took one photo I actually like.

content.headline: You almost turned back at the door
content.recap: You went to the photography society's first walk in Sham Shui Po. You almost turned back at the door but stayed, Wing showed you how she shoots shop signs at night, and you took one photo you actually like.

analysis.title: The hardest part was the door
analysis.text: It might be that the moment before walking in is the hardest part for you, and you got through it.
analysis.quote: I almost turned back at the door

analysis.title: Doing something together
analysis.text: Talking was easier when there was something to do with your hands and eyes.
analysis.quote: I took one photo I actually like

challenge.cause: You did the hard thing. The only risk is not going back next time.

advice.text: Go to the next walk too, and show Wing the photo you liked.
advice.why: Friendships grow from doing things again and again.

content.encouragement: You stayed when you wanted to leave. That's the whole skill, really.

steps.text: Sign up for the next photo walk
steps.why: Again is how it becomes yours.

steps.text: Send Wing the photo you liked
Print or save your favourite shot
steps.why: Keep the proof that you went.

entries.text: Friday night alone in my room. Everyone's stories are high table dinners and hall parties. I know it's only the highlights, but it still feels like everyone found their place except me.

content.headline: Another Friday night in your room
content.recap: You spent Friday night alone in your room while stories showed dinners and hall parties. You know it's only the highlights, but it still feels like everyone found their place except you.

analysis.title: Stories make Fridays heavier
analysis.text: It might be that Friday-night scrolling turns a quiet evening into a comparison.
analysis.quote: it still feels like everyone found their place except me

analysis.title: You already see the trick
analysis.text: You noticed it's only the highlights. That awareness is useful, even when the feeling stays.
analysis.quote: I know it's only the highlights

challenge.issue: Comparing your night with everyone's highlights
challenge.cause: Stories show the best ten seconds of other people's evenings, so a quiet night can look lonelier than it is.

advice.text: Plan next Friday in advance: the photo walk, a call with a friend, or a film you've been saving. A planned quiet night feels different from an empty one.
advice.why: Unplanned Fridays seem to be when comparing hits hardest.

content.encouragement: You went to the photo walk last week even though this feeling was there. You're not standing still.

steps.text: Put one plan in your calendar for next Friday
Turn off stories notifications for the weekend
Reply to Wing's message from the walk

entries.text: Second photo walk. Wing saved me a seat on the minibus and said “thought you'd come”. Such a small thing. After weeks of feeling alone, it made my whole day.

content.headline: Someone saved you a seat
content.recap: On the second photo walk, Wing saved you a seat on the minibus and said “thought you'd come”. After weeks of feeling alone, it made your whole day.

analysis.title: Being expected
analysis.text: It might be that what mattered most was someone expecting you to show up.
analysis.quote: thought you'd come

analysis.title: Going back worked
analysis.text: This happened because you went a second time.
analysis.quote: After weeks of feeling alone, it made my whole day

challenge.cause: A good day that grew from going back.

advice.text: Ask Wing if she'd like to grab food after the next walk.
advice.why: One friendship can grow from one seat.

content.encouragement: You went back after a hard Friday. That's why there was a seat for you.

steps.text: Ask Wing to get food after the next walk
Write down how it felt to be expected
Edit your favourite photo from today

entries.text: Accounting midterm next week. People in my class already talk about Big 4 internships like it's obvious. I sat there thinking: is this really what I want, or just what I'm supposed to want?

content.headline: Is business really yours?
content.recap: With an accounting midterm next week, people in your class already talk about Big 4 internships like it's obvious. You wondered whether this is what you want, or what you're supposed to want.

analysis.title: Other people's certainty
analysis.text: Their confidence might be making your uncertainty feel like a problem, when it's just an honest question.
analysis.quote: like it's obvious

analysis.title: The sharper question
analysis.text: You separated what you want from what you're supposed to want. That's a question worth keeping.
analysis.quote: is this really what I want, or just what I'm supposed to want?

challenge.issue: Comparing your certainty with your classmates'
challenge.cause: Talk about internships makes one path look like the only one, so not wanting it yet feels like falling behind.

advice.text: Don't decide anything about your major this week. Notice which parts of your week you enjoy, inside or outside business, and write them down.
advice.why: You asked what you want; evidence from your own week helps.

content.encouragement: You asked yourself a hard question in the middle of a busy week. That's how direction starts.

steps.text: Write down two moments you enjoyed this week
Study 40 minutes for the midterm, then stop

content.headline: The group chat went quiet again
content.recap: Your old group chat has been silent for a week. Hei posts photos, Ching is busy, and you typed a message three times and deleted it. You miss having people who just know you.

analysis.title: Missing being known
analysis.text: It might be the ease of old friends you miss most: not having to explain yourself.

analysis.title: Holding back the message

advice.text: Send the message, even a short one. A photo from your week is enough.

entries.text: Spent the whole evening editing photos from Saturday's walk. Started at eight and suddenly it was midnight. Wing said my shot of the dai pai dong lights was her favourite. I printed three and stuck them above my desk.

content.title: The evening that disappeared
content.headline: The evening that disappeared
content.body:
Hey {{name}},

You sat down to edit Saturday's photos at eight, and the next time you looked up it was midnight. Nobody asked you to do it, and nothing was due.

That's worth noticing. Most of your nights this term have been about other people: the kids on Tuesdays, Wing, the guy at the door. This one was just you and the dai pai dong lights, and the hours went by without you checking. Three of those photos are on the wall above your desk now, which says something on its own.

Talk tonight,
Your friend

entries.text: Midterms. I enjoy the psychology elective more than any business course. Does that mean I chose wrong? Or is there a way to combine them? I don't want to quit, I just want it to feel like mine.

content.headline: The major question came back
content.recap: During midterms you noticed you enjoy the psychology elective more than any business course. You wondered whether that means you chose wrong, or whether there's a way to combine them. You don't want to quit; you want it to feel like yours.

analysis.title: Ownership, not escape
analysis.text: It might be that what you want isn't a different major, but a version of this one that feels like yours.
analysis.quote: I just want it to feel like mine

analysis.title: A both-and question
analysis.text: You're asking about combining, not choosing. That opens more doors than a yes or no.
analysis.quote: Or is there a way to combine them?

challenge.cause: Midterms make every course feel like a verdict, and the elective you enjoy makes the contrast sharper.

advice.text: Talk to one senior student who combined business with something else, and ask how they did it.
advice.why: Real examples beat guessing.

content.encouragement: You didn't jump to quitting. You asked a more careful question.

entries.text: Three months ago I ate lunch alone and wondered if I was in the wrong place. Now I have Wing and the Saturday walks and the kids on Tuesdays. I still don't know what job I want. But I know I like helping people figure things out. Maybe that's enough of a direction for now.

content.headline: You don't need the whole map yet
content.recap: You looked back three months, to eating lunch alone and wondering if you were in the wrong place. Now you have Wing, the Saturday walks and the kids on Tuesdays. You still don't know what job you want, but you know you like helping people figure things out.

analysis.title: A direction, not a destination
analysis.text: It might be that knowing what you like doing is a more useful compass than a job title right now.
analysis.quote: I like helping people figure things out

analysis.title: You built this
analysis.text: The people and routines you have now came from small choices you made, one at a time.
analysis.quote: Maybe that's enough of a direction for now

challenge.cause: You're looking back with clear eyes. Let yourself see it.

advice.text: Over the break, try one more thing that involves helping people learn, and see if the feeling holds.
advice.why: Directions get clearer by testing them.

content.encouragement: In your first weeks you didn't know where to start. You started anyway, and kept going.
